tasks.description: Use a list comprehension to create a list of squares for numbers 1 to 5. Print it.
tasks.hint:
List comprehension syntax: `[expression for variable in iterable]`
`[x**2 for x in range(1, 6)]` → `[1, 4, 9, 16, 25]`
This is equivalent to a for loop that appends to a list, but in one line.
tasks.solution:
squares = [x ** 2 for x in range(1, 6)]
print(squares)
tasks.walkthrough:
For each `x` from 1 to 5, the expression `x ** 2` is worked out and collected into a new list.
It's the same as a loop that appends each square, just shorter.

tasks.description: Use a list comprehension to get only the even numbers from 1 to 10. Print the list.
tasks.hint:
Add a filter with `if` at the end: `[x for x in range(1, 11) if x % 2 == 0]`
The `if` condition acts as a filter — only items where it's True are included.
Result: `[2, 4, 6, 8, 10]`
tasks.solution:
evens = [x for x in range(1, 11) if x % 2 == 0]
print(evens)
tasks.walkthrough:
The `if` at the end acts as a filter: only numbers where the remainder after dividing by 2 is 0 get through.
The expression at the front is just `x`, so the numbers are kept as they are.

tasks.description: Given `words = ['hello', 'world', 'python', 'is', 'fun']`, use a list comprehension to get only words longer than 3 characters.
tasks.hint:
`len(word)` gives the number of characters in a string.
Filter condition: `if len(word) > 3`
`[word for word in words if len(word) > 3]` → `['hello', 'world', 'python']`
tasks.solution:
words = ['hello', 'world', 'python', 'is', 'fun']
long_words = [word for word in words if len(word) > 3]
print(long_words)
tasks.walkthrough:
`len(word)` measures each word. Only those longer than three characters pass the filter.
'is' and 'fun' are too short, so they're left out.

tasks.description: Given `nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]`, print the list reversed (last item first) without changing the original.
tasks.hint:
Slicing with a step of `-1` reverses a list: `nums[::-1]`
This creates a NEW list — the original `nums` is unchanged.
Alternative: `list(reversed(nums))` does the same thing.
tasks.walkthrough:
A slice with an empty start and stop and a step of -1 walks the whole list backwards.
It produces a new list, so `nums` itself stays in the original order.

tasks.description: Given `nums = [3, 7, 2, 9, 1, 5]`, print the maximum and minimum values on separate lines.
tasks.hint:
`max(nums)` returns the largest value, `min(nums)` returns the smallest.
Two separate `print()` calls: `print(max(nums))` then `print(min(nums))`
These are built-in functions — no import needed.
tasks.walkthrough:
`max()` and `min()` are built in and work on any list of numbers.
Two separate prints put the answers on two lines, as the checker expects.

tasks.description: Combine lists [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6] into one list using the + operator and print it.
tasks.hint:
The `+` operator on lists creates a new combined list — it doesn't modify either original.
`[1, 2, 3] + [4, 5, 6]` → `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`
Alternative: `.extend()` adds all items from one list into another in-place.
tasks.walkthrough:
`+` on two lists makes a new list with all the items of the first followed by all the items of the second.
Neither original is changed.

tasks.description: Given `nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`, use a list comprehension to create a new list where every number is doubled.
tasks.hint:
The expression in a comprehension transforms each item: `[x * 2 for x in nums]`
This creates a NEW list — `nums` stays unchanged.
Result: `[2, 4, 6, 8, 10]`
tasks.solution:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
doubled = [n * 2 for n in nums]
print(doubled)
tasks.walkthrough:
The expression `n * 2` is applied to each item in turn.
The result is a fresh list; `nums` still holds the original values.

lesson.intro:
You already know how to build a list with a loop and `.append()`. A list
comprehension does the same job in one readable line. Once it clicks, you'll
find yourself using it constantly. Today also covers a few list tools you
haven't met yet.

sections.heading: From loop to comprehension
sections.body:
Here's the loop version and the comprehension version side by side. They
produce the same list. The comprehension reads as "x squared, for each x in
the range".
sections.code:
squares = []
for x in range(1, 6):
    squares.append(x ** 2)
print(squares)

squares = [x ** 2 for x in range(1, 6)]
print(squares)

sections.heading: Adding a filter
sections.body:
Put an `if` at the end to keep only some items. The expression at the front
decides what goes in; the `if` decides which items qualify.
sections.code:
evens = [x for x in range(1, 11) if x % 2 == 0]
print(evens)

words = ['hello', 'world', 'python', 'is', 'fun']
long_words = [w for w in words if len(w) > 3]
print(long_words)

sections.heading: Transforming every item
sections.body:
The expression can be anything. Double each number, uppercase each word,
whatever you need. The original list is untouched.
sections.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print([n * 2 for n in nums])
print([w.upper() for w in ['a', 'b']])
print(nums)

sections.heading: Useful list tools
sections.body:
`max()` and `min()` find the largest and smallest. `+` joins two lists into
a new one. A slice with step -1, `nums[::-1]`, gives a reversed copy.

watch_out: The order inside the brackets is expression first, then `for`, then `if`. `[x for x in nums if x > 2]`, not `[if x > 2 ...]`.
Using the wrong brackets. Square brackets make a list; round brackets make a generator (you'll meet those later).
`nums.reverse()` reverses in place and returns `None`. Use `nums[::-1]` or `reversed()` when you want a copy.
A comprehension builds a new list. If you want to keep it, assign it to a name.
